title: 5.3 · Bits and pixels (How computers store things)
name: Bits and pixels (How computers store things)
summary: Students learn that a computer keeps everything, numbers, letters and pictures, as on/off switches called bits in storage, and that a photo is still in storage when the tablet is off. In Inside the Machine's Bits & Pixels they turn binary cards into numbers, make a picture from 0s and 1s and send a letter with five switches. Pairs share one device.
iCan: explain how the parts of a device and its software work together to keep a photo as 0s and 1s
show how the software tells the screen which pixels to light
materials: binary cards (16 8 4 2 1), one set for the board and one per pair
8 by 8 pixel grids (for the twin or the block day)
doNow: Send the word HI across the room with only a flashlight that turns on and off. How?
plan: Explore: binary cards, then where the photo lives

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 5.2, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 5.2

do: Give five students the binary cards 16 8 4 2 1. Face up is on (1), face down is off (0). Make the class's grade number together, then the number of students in the room.
Open Inside the Machine at Bits & Pixels on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Play level 1 with the class.
say: Everything in a computer is numbers, and every number is on/off switches called bits.
The bits are kept in storage, so your photo is still there when the tablet is off.
ask: Where is the photo when the tablet is switched off?
explore.afterAsk: Take answers until someone says storage. Draw the path on the board: touch sensor, processor, storage, screen. The photo lives in storage the whole time; the screen only shows it.
explore.bigIdea: Computers keep everything as on/off bits in storage, even when they are switched off.

play.pairs: driver and navigator on one device; swap at the chime every 2 levels; the navigator holds the binary cards and checks the answer before the driver taps
lookFors: thinking the photo lives in the screen
adding the cards that are face down
reading the cards from the wrong end
play.misconception: The picture is not kept in the screen: the screen only shows it, and the bits that make it are kept in storage.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: How many numbers can 5 cards make?
When the tablet is off, where is your photo, and how is it kept?
showMe: Five students hold the binary cards at the front; the class calls out a number and they flip to show it.

exit.sentencePrompt: When the tablet is off, where is your photo, and what is it made of?
exit.frame: When the tablet is off my photo is ___.

rubric.line: Storage: how a computer keeps a photo
levels: Says the photo is kept somewhere in the tablet
Says the photo is kept in storage
Also says it is kept as bits (on/off), or how it gets to the screen

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: dot-picture cards: each card shows its number as dots
the binary cards on the desk during Play
hint 1 flips one card at a time
stretch: 8-bit letters: send your initials with eight switches

unpluggedTwin.title: Binary Cards and Pixel Grids
steps: Pairs make five numbers with the binary cards and write each as 0s and 1s.
They get a row of 0s and 1s for each line of a pixel grid and color the 1s.
The finished grid shows a picture; pairs say what it is.
Each pair writes a small picture of their own as 0s and 1s and trades with a neighbor to color.
Share: where would this picture be kept in a tablet?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: how could you send the word HI across the room with only a flashlight that turns on and off?

Play Inside the Machine, chapter Bits & Pixels, in pairs for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 4 1 0 0. Goal: 3 levels. No warm-up and no projector needed; sign in with the login cards so the work is saved (signed out is fine only if the cards are missing). No devices or no internet? Run the unplugged twin printed below (Binary Cards and Pixel Grids, 15 minutes), then talk about the two discussion questions for 5 minutes.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: How many numbers can 5 cards make?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut

add: the Binary Cards and Pixel Grids twin (15 minutes) before Play
10 minutes of the Unit 5 review on Brain Board

notes: The exit evidence for this band is storage and the system, not binary; binary is enrichment.
Digits in game text are spaced, like 255 0 128.
Most pairs reach level 4 of 5 in 18 minutes: that is success.
Shared devices: this is an odd lesson in the unit, so partner A signs in; the gradebook and the Standards tab count the signed-in student.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: Send the word HI across the room with only a flashlight that turns on and off. How?

Big idea: Computers keep everything as on/off bits in storage, even when they are switched off.

We will talk about:
- How many numbers can 5 cards make?
- When the tablet is off, where is your photo, and how is it kept?

steps.title: Warm-up (live)
steps.body: Five quick questions. Your teacher shows them on the projector or starts them live.

steps.title: Play: Bits & Pixels
steps.body:
Goal: 3 levels. Stretch: finish the chapter, then 3 stars.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 4 1 0 0.
Pairs: driver and navigator. Swap when you hear the chime. The navigator checks with the paper cards.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about bits, pixels and storage.

steps.title: In your own words
steps.body:
